title: Bismuth is radioactive, with a half-life a billion times the age of the universe

cover.alt: A rainbow-coloured bismuth crystal with stepped, hopper-shaped faces.

body: Bismuth was long listed as the heaviest stable element, but in 2003 researchers at Orsay in France detected its only natural isotope, bismuth-209, decaying by alpha emission into thallium-205. Its half-life is about **2.01 × 10^19 years**, roughly a billion times the age of the universe, so almost none of it has decayed since Earth formed. The rainbow colours of the famous lab-grown crystals come from a thin oxide skin whose varying thickness makes reflected light interfere. Bismuth melts at just 271.5 °C, expands by 3.32% as it solidifies, and is unusually non-toxic for a heavy metal, which is why it stands in for lead in shotgun pellets and solder and is the bismuth in bismuth subsalicylate, the pink stomach remedy.

slides.prompt: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. How much of its original bismuth-209 has decayed so far?
slides.answer: About one atom in six billion
slides.detail: With a half-life of 2.01 × 10^19 years, the decay is so slow that for every practical purpose bismuth behaves as a stable element.

slides.label: the half-life of bismuth-209, over a billion times the age of the universe
slides.text: The decay was finally detected in 2003 at the Institut d’astrophysique spatiale in Orsay, France.

steps.label: A thin oxide film forms on the surface
Light reflects off the film’s top and base
Film thickness sets the colour you see

left.label: Lead
left.text: Toxic: being replaced in shotgun pellets, which poison wetland birds, and in solder under EU lead-reduction rules.

right.label: Bismuth
right.text: Unusually low toxicity for a heavy metal, so bismuth–tin shot and bismuth solders take lead’s place, and bismuth subsalicylate is the pink stomach remedy.

slides.question: Why are bismuth crystals rainbow-coloured?
slides.explanation: Variations in the thickness of the oxide layer on the surface make reflected light waves interfere, so different thicknesses show different colours, like oil on water.
